extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate contestants of the William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition (mathematically mature problem solvers comfortable with proofs)
extracted.subtask_description: The 78th William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition problem list (A1–A6, B1–B6): twelve proof-style problems requiring rigorous solutions, constructions, or exact counts. Each item specifies what a correct solution must produce (identification, proof, count, evaluation, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: A1 — description of the set S and membership question
rubrics_metrics.description: Let S be the smallest set of positive integers such that (a) 2 is in S, (b) n is in S whenever n^2 is in S, and (c) (n + 5)^2 is in S whenever n is in S. Which positive integers are not in S? (The set S is “smallest” in the sense that S is contained in any other such set.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a rigorous characterization of S (or its complement) and a proof that all and only the claimed integers satisfy the membership/nonmembership conditions, using the closure properties and minimality of S.

rubrics_metrics.name: A2 — integer-coefficient polynomial property of Qn(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Q0(x) = 1, Q1(x) = x, and Qn(x) = (Q_{n-1}(x))^2 - 1 over Q_{n-2}(x) for all n ≥ 2. Show that, whenever n is a positive integer, Qn(x) is equal to a polynomial with integer coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show by induction or algebraic manipulation that each Q_n is a polynomial (no denominator remains) and that the coefficients are integers; supply a proof (e.g., using divisibility relations, recurrence properties, or known families of orthogonal polynomials).

rubrics_metrics.name: A3 — monotonicity and divergence of the integral sequence In
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a and b be real numbers with a < b, and let f and g be continuous functions from [a, b] to (0, ∞) such that ∫_a^b f(x) dx = ∫_a^b g(x) dx but f ≠ g. For every positive integer n, define I_n = ∫_a^b (f(x))^{n+1} / (g(x))^{n} dx. Show that I1, I2, I3, . . . is an increasing sequence with lim_{n→∞} I_n = ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a rigorous argument that I_{n+1} ≥ I_n for all n, and that I_n tends to infinity (likely by finding a set where f>g and exploiting exponential growth of the integrand), using continuity and positivity assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: A4 — partition into two equal-average groups
rubrics_metrics.description: A class with 2N students took a quiz, on which the possible scores were 0,1,...,10. Each of these scores occurred at least once, and the average score was exactly 7.4. Show that the class can be divided into two groups of N students in such a way that the average score for each group was exactly 7.4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct or prove existence of a partition of the multiset of scores into two equal-size submultisets with the same average (hence same sum). Provide a rigorous combinatorial or averaging/continuity argument (e.g., pairing, discrete intermediate value or swapping argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: A5 — existence of n giving highest winning probability for each player
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the integers from 1 to n is written on a separate card, the cards are shuffled. Three players A, B, and C take turns in order A, B, C, A, ... choosing one card at random from the deck. After a card is chosen, that card and all higher-numbered cards are removed from the deck, and the remaining cards are reshuffled before the next turn. Play continues until someone draws card 1. Show that for each of the three players, there are arbitrarily large values of n for which that player has the highest probability among the three players of winning the game.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each player (A,B,C) produce an infinite sequence of n values for which that player’s winning probability exceeds the other two; provide explicit constructions or asymptotic/probability arguments and rigorous comparison of probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: A6 — count edge-colorings of a labeled icosahedron with local face constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: The 30 edges of a regular icosahedron are distinguished by labeling them 1,2,...,30. How many different ways are there to paint each edge red, white, or blue such that each of the 20 triangular faces of the icosahedron has two edges of the same color and a third edge of a different color?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count all colorings of the labeled edges satisfying the local constraint on every triangular face. Provide a combinatorial enumeration or bijection, and a rigorous justification that all counted colorings meet the facewise constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: B1 — characterization of intersecting lines via vector scaling property
rubrics_metrics.description: Let L1 and L2 be distinct lines in the plane. Prove that L1 and L2 intersect if and only if, for every real number λ ≠ 0 and every point P not on L1 or L2, there exist points A1 on L1 and A2 on L2 such that →PA2 = λ →PA1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a proof of the equivalence: show that if the lines intersect then for any λ and P such A1,A2 exist, and conversely show that if they do not intersect then the property fails for some λ or P. Use vector geometry or coordinate arguments with rigorous justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: B2 — minimal starting term a for special representable N
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose that a positive integer N can be expressed as the sum of k consecutive positive integers N = a + (a+1) + ... + (a+k−1) for k = 2017 but for no other values of k > 1. Considering all positive integers N with this property, what is the smallest positive integer a that occurs in any of these expressions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze representations of integers as sums of consecutive integers, use number-theoretic constraints on k and a, and identify the minimal possible starting term a across all N with the stated uniqueness property; give a rigorous justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: B3 — irrationality of f(1/2) given power-series constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose that f(x) = Σ_{i=0}^∞ c_i x^i is a power series for which each coefficient c_i is 0 or 1. Show that if f(2/3) = 3/2, then f(1/2) must be irrational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use properties of digital expansions or rationality criteria for power series with 0/1 coefficients to deduce a contradiction if f(1/2) were rational; provide a rigorous argument linking the given value at 2/3 to the nature of the coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: B4 — evaluation of an alternating logarithmic infinite series
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the sum 3 · Σ_{k=0}^∞ [ ln(4k+2)/(4k+2) − ln(4k+3)/(4k+3) − ln(4k+4)/(4k+4) − ln(4k+5)/(4k+5) ] = 3·(ln 2/2 − ln 3/3 − ln 4/4 − ln 5/5 + ln 6/6 − ln 7/7 − ... ) (as written in the exam).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce a closed-form value of the infinite series (using known series, telescoping, integral representations, or manipulations with the logarithm), with a rigorous derivation and justification of convergence and term rearrangements if used.

rubrics_metrics.name: B5 — triangle with exactly two distinct equalizers and minimal largest side
rubrics_metrics.description: A line in the plane of a triangle T is called an equalizer if it divides T into two regions having equal area and equal perimeter. Find positive integers a > b > c, with a as small as possible, such that there exists a triangle with side lengths a,b,c that has exactly two distinct equalizers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct or prove existence of a triangle with integer side lengths (a,b,c) meeting the equalizer-count requirement, identify minimal a, and rigorously show there are exactly two distinct equalizers for that triangle and no smaller a works.

rubrics_metrics.name: B6 — count ordered 64-tuples with distinct entries and divisibility condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the number of ordered 64-tuples (x0,x1,...,x63) such that x0,...,x63 are distinct elements of {1,2,...,2017} and x0 + x1 + 2x2 + 3x3 + · · · + 63 x63 is divisible by 2017.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an exact count (closed form) of ordered 64-tuples satisfying distinctness and the modular divisibility condition; use combinatorial, group-theoretic, or number-theoretic arguments (e.g., symmetry, properties of residues modulo prime 2017) with full justification.
